children.text: T1: Thermal lens

An intense laser beam incident on a semitransparent plate can self-focus behind it because inhomogeneous heating changes the refractive index. Consider material with positive thermo-optic coefficient \(\gamma=dn/dT\).

A semitransparent disk has radius \(a=15.0\,\mathrm{mm}\), thickness \(b=0.2\,\mathrm{mm}\), optical absorption coefficient \(A=0.1\), thermal conductivity \(k=0.3\,\mathrm{W\,m^{-1}K^{-1}}\), and \(\gamma=2.5\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{K^{-1}}\). Its outer rim is thermally connected to a circular metallic holder maintained at \(T_h=20^\circ\mathrm C\). A parallel laser beam of radius \(\sigma=0.5\,\mathrm{mm}\) and power \(P_L=20\,\mathrm{mW}\) falls normally on the disk centre, with uniform intensity across its cross-section.

nodes.alt: Original thermal-lens setup: laser beam of radius sigma passes through a thin disk of radius a and thickness b, then converges behind it. The metallic rim holder is omitted.

children.text: a
Sketch the qualitative temperature profile \(T(r)\), where \(r\) is distance from the beam axis. Clearly mark the illuminated region \(0\le r\le\sigma\) and outer region \(\sigma\le r\le a\).
b
Near the centre, \(T(r)=T_c+mr^2\). Calculate \(T_c\) and \(m\).
c
Show that the beam focuses at one point and find its distance \(f\) from the disk. If you did not find \(T_c\) and \(m\), you may use them as parameters in the final answer.
Ignore thermal expansion, radiation and heat exchange with the air. Take the refractive index of air as \(n_{\rm air}=1\).

statement.text:
T1: Thermal lens
An intense laser beam incident on a semitransparent plate can self-focus behind it because inhomogeneous heating changes the refractive index. Consider material with positive thermo-optic coefficient \(\gamma=dn/dT\).
A semitransparent disk has radius \(a=15.0\,\mathrm{mm}\), thickness \(b=0.2\,\mathrm{mm}\), optical absorption coefficient \(A=0.1\), thermal conductivity \(k=0.3\,\mathrm{W\,m^{-1}K^{-1}}\), and \(\gamma=2.5\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{K^{-1}}\). Its outer rim is thermally connected to a circular metallic holder maintained at \(T_h=20^\circ\mathrm C\). A parallel laser beam of radius \(\sigma=0.5\,\mathrm{mm}\) and power \(P_L=20\,\mathrm{mW}\) falls normally on the disk centre, with uniform intensity across its cross-section.

a
Sketch the qualitative temperature profile \(T(r)\), where \(r\) is distance from the beam axis. Clearly mark the illuminated region \(0\le r\le\sigma\) and outer region \(\sigma\le r\le a\).
b
Near the centre, \(T(r)=T_c+mr^2\). Calculate \(T_c\) and \(m\).
c
Show that the beam focuses at one point and find its distance \(f\) from the disk. If you did not find \(T_c\) and \(m\), you may use them as parameters in the final answer.
Ignore thermal expansion, radiation and heat exchange with the air. Take the refractive index of air as \(n_{\rm air}=1\).

children.text: T1: Thermal lens
a. Temperature profile

The profile has a horizontal tangent at \(r=0\), is decreasing and concave down within the beam, decreasing and convex outside it, and reaches \(T_h\) with a nonzero negative slope at \(a\). Temperature and slope match at \(r=\sigma\).

nodes.alt: Original temperature profile T(r), labelled Tc and Th, showing horizontal central tangent, concave illuminated region ending at sigma, convex outer region ending at a, and a nonzero negative rim slope.

children.text: b. Radial heat flow
At steady state, the absorbed power inside radius \(r\) flows out through area \(2\pi rb\). The supplied \(A\) is the dimensionless absorbed fraction, so
\[-2\pi kbr\frac{dT}{dr}=P_{\rm abs}(r),\qquad P_{\rm abs}(r)=\begin{cases}AP_Lr^2/\sigma^2,&0\le r\le\sigma,\\ AP_L,&\sigma\le r\le a.\end{cases}\]
Integrating inside and outside, with \(T(0)=T_c\) and \(T(a)=T_h\), gives
\[T(r)=\begin{cases}T_c-\dfrac{AP_Lr^2}{4\pi kb\sigma^2},&0\le r\le\sigma,\\ T_h+\dfrac{AP_L}{2\pi kb}\ln\dfrac ar,&\sigma\le r\le a.\end{cases}\]
\[m=-\frac{AP_L}{4\pi kb\sigma^2}\simeq-1.06\times10^7\,\mathrm{K/m^2}.\]
Matching the temperatures at \(\sigma\) yields
\[T_c=T_h+\frac{AP_L}{4\pi kb}\left[1+2\ln\left(\frac a\sigma\right)\right]\simeq40.7^\circ\mathrm C\simeq41^\circ\mathrm C.\]

An alternative is to substitute the quadratic form directly into the heat-flow equation to get \(m\), and integrate \(T_c-T_h=\int_0^a P_{\rm abs}(r)/(2\pi kbr)\,dr\) piecewise to get the same central temperature. The source's intermediate absorbed-power equation omits \(A\) in one expression for the incident intensity. The consistent absorbed power includes \(A\), as above. Its marking-table match point should read \(r=\sigma\), not \(a\).
c. Fermat's principle

nodes.alt: Original paraxial ray construction through the heated disk, showing thickness b, internal bending angle phi, transverse displacement h, exit angle theta, local curvature radius R and focus distance f.

children.text: Within the beam, \(n(0)-n(r)=\gamma|m|r^2\). In a thin plate rays travel approximately the same distance \(b\) inside the material and exit at nearly their entrance radius. The optical path to a focus at distance \(f\gg r\) is
\[s(r)\simeq bn(r)+\sqrt{f^2+r^2}\simeq bn(r)+f+\frac{r^2}{2f}.\]

A common focus requires this path to be independent of \(r\). Equivalently \(b[n(0)-n(r)]=r^2/(2f)\), or \(bn'(r)+r/f=0\). Since the index difference is quadratic, the same \(f\) works for every illuminated radius:
\[f=\frac1{2\gamma b|m|}=\frac{2\pi k\sigma^2}{\gamma AP_L}\simeq0.94\,\mathrm m.\]
Alternative: ray and wavefront tracing

Approximate a ray inside the disk by a circular arc with local radius \(R=-n/n'\). Snell's law between nearby radii gives internal bending \(\varphi\simeq-bn'/n\). Refraction into air gives \(\theta\simeq n\varphi=-bn'=2\gamma|m|br\). Thus \(f\simeq r/\theta=1/(2\gamma b|m|)\). The factor \(b\) is absent from one intermediate angle equation in the source, but is necessary dimensionally and agrees with its final focal length.

nodes.alt: Original wavefront construction for neighbouring rays at r and r+dr: perpendicular wavefront, light-speed arrows v(r) and v(r)+dv, and ray direction marked.

children.text: Alternatively, the wavefront angular speed is \(\dot\varphi=d(c/n)/dr=-cn'/n^2\), and travel time is \(bn/c\), giving the same \(\varphi=-bn'/n\). A more explicit path calculation uses \(n(r)\cos\varphi=n(r_0)\). Expanding near entrance radius \(r_0\) gives
\[-\frac{dr}{dx}\simeq\sqrt{\frac{4\gamma|m|r_0}{n(r_0)}}\sqrt{r_0-r},\qquad r(x)\simeq r_0-\frac{\gamma|m|r_0}{n(r_0)}x^2.\]

The exit angle inside the disk is \(-r'(b)\simeq2\gamma|m|r_0b/n(r_0)\). Refraction into air again gives \(\theta\simeq2\gamma|m|r_0b\), proving the same common focal point to the stated paraxial accuracy. Original partial-credit tables for all approaches are retained in the solution PDF.

solution.text:
T1: Thermal lens
a. Temperature profile
The profile has a horizontal tangent at \(r=0\), is decreasing and concave down within the beam, decreasing and convex outside it, and reaches \(T_h\) with a nonzero negative slope at \(a\). Temperature and slope match at \(r=\sigma\).

b. Radial heat flow

Integrating inside and outside, with \(T(0)=T_c\) and \(T(a)=T_h\), gives
\[T(r)=\begin{cases}T_c-\dfrac{AP_Lr^2}{4\pi kb\sigma^2},&0\le r\le\sigma,\\ T_h+\dfrac{AP_L}{2\pi kb}\ln\dfrac ar,&\sigma\le r\le a.\end{cases}\]
\[m=-\frac{AP_L}{4\pi kb\sigma^2}\simeq-1.06\times10^7\,\mathrm{K/m^2}.\]
Matching the temperatures at \(\sigma\) yields
\[T_c=T_h+\frac{AP_L}{4\pi kb}\left[1+2\ln\left(\frac a\sigma\right)\right]\simeq40.7^\circ\mathrm C\simeq41^\circ\mathrm C.\]
An alternative is to substitute the quadratic form directly into the heat-flow equation to get \(m\), and integrate \(T_c-T_h=\int_0^a P_{\rm abs}(r)/(2\pi kbr)\,dr\) piecewise to get the same central temperature. The source's intermediate absorbed-power equation omits \(A\) in one expression for the incident intensity. The consistent absorbed power includes \(A\), as above. Its marking-table match point should read \(r=\sigma\), not \(a\).
c. Fermat's principle

Within the beam, \(n(0)-n(r)=\gamma|m|r^2\). In a thin plate rays travel approximately the same distance \(b\) inside the material and exit at nearly their entrance radius. The optical path to a focus at distance \(f\gg r\) is
\[s(r)\simeq bn(r)+\sqrt{f^2+r^2}\simeq bn(r)+f+\frac{r^2}{2f}.\]
A common focus requires this path to be independent of \(r\). Equivalently \(b[n(0)-n(r)]=r^2/(2f)\), or \(bn'(r)+r/f=0\). Since the index difference is quadratic, the same \(f\) works for every illuminated radius:
\[f=\frac1{2\gamma b|m|}=\frac{2\pi k\sigma^2}{\gamma AP_L}\simeq0.94\,\mathrm m.\]

Approximate a ray inside the disk by a circular arc with local radius \(R=-n/n'\). Snell's law between nearby radii gives internal bending \(\varphi\simeq-bn'/n\). Refraction into air gives \(\theta\simeq n\varphi=-bn'=2\gamma|m|br\). Thus \(f\simeq r/\theta=1/(2\gamma b|m|)\). The factor \(b\) is absent from one intermediate angle equation in the source, but is necessary dimensionally and agrees with its final focal length.

Alternatively, the wavefront angular speed is \(\dot\varphi=d(c/n)/dr=-cn'/n^2\), and travel time is \(bn/c\), giving the same \(\varphi=-bn'/n\). A more explicit path calculation uses \(n(r)\cos\varphi=n(r_0)\). Expanding near entrance radius \(r_0\) gives
\[-\frac{dr}{dx}\simeq\sqrt{\frac{4\gamma|m|r_0}{n(r_0)}}\sqrt{r_0-r},\qquad r(x)\simeq r_0-\frac{\gamma|m|r_0}{n(r_0)}x^2.\]
